subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Ingroup Bias
description: Learn Ingroup Bias in one minute.

hook.text: Kids sorted by T-shirt color instantly favored their own group and distrusted the other. In minutes.

buildup.text: Tajfel's minimal group studies showed favoritism even when groups were assigned randomly by coin flip.

discovery.text: Ingroup bias: we favor people we see as part of our group and distrust those we see as outsiders.

twist.text: The definition of 'our group' is flexible. Shared nationality, team, company, or even a T-shirt color works.

climax.text: Most discrimination isn't active hate. It's passive preference for familiar faces and shared labels.

punchline.text: We don't hate outsiders. We just love insiders more.

quiz.question: What did Tajfel's studies reveal?
options: Group favoritism only occurs with real rivalries
Random group assignment still creates ingroup bias
Ingroup bias requires years of shared experience

details.summary: Ingroup bias is the tendency to favor members of your own group over outsiders, giving them more trust, generosity, and positive interpretations of their behavior. Even arbitrary group assignments in laboratory settings trigger measurable ingroup favoritism.
details.whyItMatters: Ingroup bias drives discrimination, tribalism, and conflict. It operates automatically and unconsciously, distorting hiring decisions, resource allocation, and social judgment even among people who genuinely believe they are fair and impartial.
takeaways: People favor their own group even when group membership is arbitrary
Ingroup bias distorts hiring, promotion, and resource allocation decisions
Minimal group experiments show bias requires no history of conflict

faq.question: How quickly does ingroup bias form?
faq.answer: Instantly. In the minimal group paradigm, people assigned to groups based on coin flips immediately favor their group over the other. No shared history, conflict, or meaningful difference is needed. Mere categorization triggers favoritism.

faq.question: Can ingroup bias be reduced in organizations?
faq.answer: Creating superordinate identities that encompass both groups helps. Cross-group collaboration on shared goals, diverse teams, and structured decision processes that anonymize group membership all reduce but do not eliminate the bias.
